name: Wheezing
preview_text: เสียงหายใจดังเสียงฮืดและสีของเสมหะจะบอกผู้ประกอบวิชาชีพ TCM ได้อย่างแน่ชัดว่าระบบอวัยวะใดไม่สมดุล และสมุนไพรเฉพาะจุดและการฝังเข็มมักจะทำให้สังเกตเห็นได้ชัดเจน...

synonyms: ["Breathing With Wheezes", "Whistling Breath", "Wheezing or laboured breathing", "Mild wheezing", "Slight wheezing", "Slight wheezing in severe cases", "Wheezing on Exertion", "Slight wheezing on exertion", "Chronic Wheezing"]
conventional_description:
Wheezing is a high-pitched whistling sound that occurs when air struggles to pass through narrowed or obstructed airways. It is most commonly associated with asthma, but can also arise from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), bronchitis, allergies, or respiratory infections.
In conventional medicine, wheezing is assessed through a physical exam, listening to the lungs with a stethoscope, and often confirmed with pulmonary function tests like spirometry. The narrowing of the airways can be due to inflammation, excess mucus, or bronchial muscle constriction.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment focuses on relieving airway constriction and reducing inflammation. Quick-relief medications like short-acting bronchodilators (e.g., albuterol) are used for acute symptoms, while long-term control may involve inhaled corticosteroids, long-acting bronchodilators, leukotriene modifiers, or biologic therapies. Avoidance of known triggers - allergens, smoke, cold air - is also a cornerstone of management.
tcm_understanding:
The Lungs are the primary organ involved in wheezing, responsible for descending and dispersing Qi throughout the body. When this function is disrupted - by phlegm, cold, or heat - the airway becomes obstructed and the breath turns into a whistling, rattling sound. Crucially, the phlegm that clogs the Lungs is often produced by a weak Spleen, which fails to transform fluids properly, allowing Dampness to accumulate and congeal.
In excess patterns, phlegm is the main culprit. Cold-Phlegm creates a high-pitched, tight wheeze with white, frothy sputum, while Phlegm-Heat causes a loud, gurgling wheeze with sticky yellow phlegm. Damp-Phlegm produces a heavy, rattling sound with copious white mucus. In deficiency patterns, the wheeze is quieter and worsens with exertion - the Lungs lack the Qi to push air out, or the Kidneys fail to 'grasp' the breath, leaving it stuck in the chest.
This is why the same Western diagnosis of asthma can have so many different TCM presentations. A practitioner listens to the quality of the wheeze, examines the phlegm, and checks the tongue and pulse to identify the underlying pattern. Treatment isn't about temporarily opening the airways - it's about correcting the specific imbalance that causes the wheezing in the first place.
classical_quote: 「咳而上气，喉中水鸡声，射干麻黄汤主之。」
classical_translation: "Cough with dyspnea, with a sound like water-fowl in the throat, Shegan Mahuang Decoction governs it. This is the earliest classical description of wheezing due to Cold-Phlegm in the Lungs."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by listening to the quality of the wheeze and asking about the sputum. A high-pitched, whistling sound and white, foamy phlegm that worsens in cold air points toward Cold-Phlegm in the Lungs. The tongue is pale with a thin, slippery white coat, and the pulse feels tight or floating-tight, like a rope pulled taut. This pattern often strikes after exposure to wind-cold.
When the wheeze is loud and coarse, accompanied by yellow, sticky sputum and a sensation of heat in the chest, Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs is likely. The person feels thirsty, the face may be flushed, and the tongue appears red with a yellow, greasy coating. The pulse is rapid and slippery, like beads rolling. This pattern is aggravated by hot weather or rich, spicy foods.
In Damp-Phlegm in the Lungs, the wheezing is accompanied by copious, sticky sputum that is difficult to cough out. The chest feels heavy and congested, and the tongue has a thick, greasy coating while the pulse is slippery. This pattern develops gradually from a diet heavy in dairy, greasy foods, or from a weak Spleen that fails to transform fluids, causing phlegm to accumulate chronically.
When wheezing appears mainly on exertion and is accompanied by a weak voice, shortness of breath, and spontaneous sweating, Lung Qi Deficiency is the underlying pattern. The person catches colds easily and feels drained. The tongue is pale with a thin white coat, and the pulse is weak and thready. This is a remission-phase pattern where the Lung lacks the strength to descend and disperse Qi properly.
If chronic mild wheezing comes with fatigue, poor appetite, loose stools, and a sensation of heaviness, Spleen and Lung Qi Deficiency is present. The Spleen fails to transform fluids, generating phlegm that weakens the Lung further. The tongue is pale, often with tooth marks on the sides, and the pulse is weak. This pattern reflects a cycle where poor digestion feeds respiratory weakness.
Wheezing that worsens dramatically with even slight exertion, along with a deep, weak pulse, sore lower back, cold limbs, and sometimes edema, indicates Kidneys failing to receive Qi. The Kidney is too weak to grasp the Lung Qi downward, so breath becomes shallow and labored. The tongue is pale and swollen, and the pulse is deep and thready. This pattern often appears in long-standing asthma or in the elderly.

patterns.symptoms: ["White, foamy or watery sputum", "Rattling or gurgling sound in the throat", "Feeling cold and chilly, cold hands and feet", "No thirst, preference for warm drinks", "Chest tightness and stuffiness", "Wheezing worsens with cold exposure"]
patterns.worse_with: Cold weather or drafts, Cold or raw foods and drinks, Dairy and greasy foods, Lying completely flat, Overexertion or heavy exercise
patterns.better_with: Warmth and covering up, Warm ginger tea or drinks, Steam inhalation, Light, warm, cooked foods, Rest in a semi-reclined position
patterns.why_this_happens:
When Wind-Cold invades the body, it can combine with existing phlegm in the Lungs. The cold congeals fluids into thick, white, foamy sputum that physically blocks the airways. As the Lung Qi tries to push through this obstruction, it creates the whistling, rattling sound of wheezing.
Because cold constricts and slows everything down, the wheezing is often accompanied by a deep chilliness and a preference for warmth. The breathing difficulty gets worse when lying flat, as the phlegm settles and further narrows the air passages.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale and swollen with a thick, white, greasy or slippery coating. Pulse: slippery and slow, possibly wiry.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold and dampness are the root of this pattern. Cold constricts the airways and congeals fluids into sticky phlegm, so external cold, cold drinks, and raw foods all make the obstruction worse. Warmth and warm, drying foods like ginger help disperse the cold and transform the phlegm, allowing Lung Qi to descend smoothly again. Dairy and greasy foods are notoriously phlegm-forming and directly add to the blockage, while lying flat lets the phlegm pool and narrow the breathing passages further.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that create more phlegm. Favor warm, cooked meals and sip ginger tea throughout the day. Keep the neck and chest covered in cool weather, and try a steam inhalation with a drop of eucalyptus oil to loosen phlegm.

patterns.symptoms: ["Loud wheezing or gurgling sounds in the throat", "Cough with copious thick yellow or green sticky sputum", "Thirst with desire to drink cold fluids", "Feeling of heat, flushed face, and restlessness", "Chest tightness and oppression"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy or fried food, Hot weather or stuffy rooms, Alcohol or smoking, Emotional stress and anger, Respiratory infections or frequent colds
patterns.better_with: Cool fresh air, Drinking cool fluids, Eating pears or radish, Gentle breathing exercises, Resting in a cool room
patterns.why_this_happens: When Heat builds up in the Lungs it thickens fluids into sticky yellow phlegm that clogs the airways. This phlegm obstructs the normal descending and dispersing of Lung Qi, trapping air and triggering loud, gurgling wheezing. The Heat also makes breathing rapid and shallow, and drives thirst and restlessness.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with a yellow greasy coating, especially thicker in the front; may have red prickles on the front third. Pulse: slippery and rapid (滑数 huá shuò), strongest at the right cun (Lung) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-Heat in the Lungs is a pattern of excess Heat and sticky phlegm. Spicy, greasy, and hot foods, alcohol, and stuffy environments add more Heat and thicken phlegm, directly aggravating the root cause. Cooling foods, fresh air, and adequate hydration help clear Heat and thin the phlegm, while deep breathing and rest support the Lung's natural descending motion, making it easier to expel the phlegm and calm the wheeze.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol, which all generate Heat and thicken phlegm. Eat cooling, phlegm-resolving foods like Asian pears, radish, water chestnuts, and loquats. Stay well hydrated with warm or room-temperature water. Keep living spaces cool and well-ventilated, and avoid smoke and strong chemical fumes.

patterns.better_with: Warm dry environment, Light, warm, cooked foods, Gentle exercise or walking, Warm ginger tea or drinks, Chest warmth
patterns.why_this_happens: When the Spleen is too weak to transform fluids properly, Dampness builds up and eventually congeals into sticky Phlegm. This Phlegm settles in the Lungs, physically obstructing the airways and making it hard for air to move freely. The result is a heavy, rattling wheeze with copious white phlegm that you can often cough up easily.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale and swollen with teeth marks, covered by a thick white greasy coating. Pulse: Slippery (滑 huá), often soggy, especially slippery at the right cun position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Dampness and Phlegm are heavy, sticky substances that congeal when the body is cold and still. Warmth and gentle movement help disperse them, like steam clearing a fog. The Spleen is the source of Phlegm, so light, easily digested meals support its function, while greasy, cold, or excessive food overwhelms it and creates more Dampness. Keeping the chest warm prevents external cold from congealing fluids in the Lungs.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid damp-producing foods: dairy, greasy fried foods, sugar, and cold raw vegetables. Eat warm, cooked meals like soups and congees that are easy to digest. Gentle daily movement like walking helps Qi flow and dries internal dampness. Keep your chest and neck warm in damp weather.

patterns.symptoms: ["Wheezing worse on exertion, better with rest", "Shortness of breath with a weak, low voice", "Spontaneous daytime sweating without heat", "Sensitivity to wind and cold, catching colds easily", "Fatigue and pale complexion"]
patterns.worse_with: Overexertion or heavy exercise, Cold weather or drafts, Cold or raw foods and drinks, Prolonged talking or singing
patterns.better_with: Rest, Warm drinks and soups, Gentle exercise or walking, Warm, still air
patterns.why_this_happens: When Lung Qi is weak, it cannot properly descend and disperse air through the breathing passages. The breath becomes shallow, and even mild exertion demands more Qi than the Lungs can supply, which triggers wheezing and shortness of breath. The weakened defensive (Wei) Qi also leaves the body vulnerable to wind and cold, making wheezing episodes more frequent after exposure.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, tender body, possible teeth marks, thin white coating. Pulse: empty or weak, especially the right Cun (Lung) position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Lung Qi is already deficient, so any demand beyond its capacity-like exercise or talking-drains it further and brings on wheezing. Cold and raw foods chill the Spleen and Lungs, making it harder to produce and circulate Qi. Rest, warmth, and gentle movement conserve Qi, while warm foods and drinks provide the mild Yang support the Lungs need to descend Qi smoothly.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, easy-to-digest foods like congee, stews, and soups with a little ginger or cinnamon to gently warm the Lungs. Avoid raw, cold, and iced foods that weaken digestive and Lung Qi. Gentle, consistent movement such as walking or qigong builds Qi without exhausting it, while overexertion and prolonged talking should be avoided.

patterns.symptoms: ["Wheezing worsens with exertion", "Fatigue and general weakness", "Poor appetite, bloating, loose stools", "Thin, watery or white phlegm", "Weak voice, reluctance to speak", "Spontaneous sweating and frequent colds"]
patterns.worse_with: Overexertion or heavy exercise, Cold, raw, or greasy foods, Cold damp weather, Stress and worry, Respiratory infections or frequent colds
patterns.better_with: Rest, Warm, easily digestible foods like congee, Gentle breathing exercises, Warm dry environment
patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is the engine that transforms food and fluids into usable Qi. When it is weak, it fails to do this properly, leaving behind a residue of dampness and phlegm that settles in the lungs. At the same time, deficient Lung Qi lacks the strength to descend and spread the breath, so the airways narrow and wheezing occurs. This creates a chronic, low-grade wheeze that worsens whenever the body is tired or the digestion is under strain.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, and tender with teeth marks, thin white slippery coating. Pulse: weak and forceless, especially the right cun (Lung) and right guan (Spleen) positions, which feel soft and become weaker with pressure.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Spleen and Lung Qi are the foundation of energy and immunity. Overexertion and stress deplete them further, making wheezing worse. Cold and damp foods directly injure the Spleen, leading to more phlegm. Rest and warm, cooked foods conserve and rebuild Qi, while gentle movement circulates it without draining reserves. Protecting the body from wind and cold shields the already weak Lung, preventing the triggers that set off wheezing.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like congee, soups, and stews. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy meals that burden the Spleen and generate phlegm. Gentle daily movement such as walking or qigong helps circulate Qi without exhausting it. Protect the neck and chest from wind and cold, and get plenty of sleep to allow Qi to rebuild.

patterns.symptoms: ["Wheezing worsens with exertion", "Difficulty breathing in, exhaling feels much easier", "Lower back and knee soreness and weakness", "Fatigue and low motivation", "Spontaneous sweating with effort"]
patterns.worse_with: Overexertion or heavy exercise, Cold weather or drafts, Chronic stress and overwork
patterns.better_with: Rest, Warmth on the lower back, Gentle breathing exercises
patterns.why_this_happens: In TCM, one of the Kidneys' key jobs is to "grasp" the Qi that the Lungs send down, pulling the breath deep into the body. When Kidney Qi is too weak to do this grasping, the breath "floats" up and gets stuck in the chest. This leads to the sensation of not being able to get a full breath in, and the wheezing or breathlessness that worsens with any effort, because exertion drains the very Qi that is already depleted.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, puffy, often with teeth marks, and a thin white moist coating. Pulse: deep and weak, especially at the rear position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Exertion and overwork drain the Kidneys and Qi further, making the wheezing immediately worse. Cold constricts and weakens the already deficient Yang. Rest and warmth, conversely, conserve and support the remaining Kidney Yang, allowing the Kidneys to better perform their function of receiving Qi.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize warm, cooked foods and avoid raw or cold items that drain Kidney Yang. Gentle, consistent movement like walking or tai chi is better than intense workouts that deplete Qi. Keep the lower back and feet warm.

It works by warming the lungs, clearing accumulated thin watery phlegm, and helping the body expel the cold. It works by opening the airways, directing Lung Qi downward, clearing heat, and resolving thick, sticky phlegm. Commonly applied for asthma and bronchitis with yellow, difficult-to-expectorate sputum.

formulas.translation: Three-Seed Decoction to Nourish One's Parents · Ming dynasty, 1522 CE
formulas.properties: Warm, Warms the Lungs and Transforms Phlegm-Fluids, Descends Qi, Stops Cough and Calms Wheezing
formulas.description: A gentle, three-herb formula made entirely from common plant seeds, originally created to help elderly parents suffering from chronic cough with heavy phlegm, chest congestion, and poor digestion. It works by dissolving accumulated phlegm in the chest, calming rebellious Qi that causes coughing and wheezing, and improving digestion to stop new phlegm from forming. Despite its simplicity, it remains one of the most widely used formulas for phlegm-related respiratory conditions.

formulas.translation: Two-Aged Herb Decoction · Sòng dynasty, 1078–1148 CE
formulas.properties: Warm, Dries Dampness and Transforms Phlegm, Regulates Qi and Harmonizes the Middle Burner, Directs Rebellious Qi Downward and Stops Vomiting
formulas.description: A foundational formula used to clear excess phlegm and dampness from the body, especially when they cause coughing with white phlegm, nausea, chest tightness, dizziness, or a heavy feeling in the limbs. It works by drying dampness, dissolving phlegm, and supporting healthy digestion. Named for its two key ingredients, Ban Xia and Chen Pi, which are most effective when aged.

formulas.translation: Tonify the Lungs Decoction · Yuán dynasty, 1331 CE
formulas.properties: Slightly Warm, Tonifies Lung Qi, Tonifies Qi and consolidates the Exterior, Astringes the Lungs and Stops Cough
formulas.description: A classical formula designed to strengthen weak lungs and support breathing. It is used for people with a long-standing weak cough, shortness of breath, a quiet or feeble voice, and a tendency to sweat easily, all signs that the Lung's Qi has become depleted over time.

formulas.translation: Jade Windscreen Powder · Yuán dynasty, ~1347 CE
formulas.properties: Slightly Warm, Tonifies Qi, Secures the Exterior, Astringes to Stop Sweating
formulas.description: A simple but highly valued three-herb formula used to strengthen the body's natural defenses against colds, flu, and allergies. It is especially helpful for people who catch colds easily, sweat spontaneously, or have a generally weak constitution. The name "Jade Windscreen" reflects its role as a precious shield against illness-causing pathogens.

formulas.translation: Six Gentlemen Decoction · Míng dynasty, 1515 CE (also recorded in the Yuán dynasty text Shi Yi De Xiao Fang, ~1337 CE)

formulas.description: A classical formula that strengthens digestion and clears away dampness and phlegm accumulation. It is used for people who experience poor appetite, bloating, loose stools, nausea, and fatigue due to a weakened digestive system that has allowed excess moisture and phlegm to build up in the body.

formulas.translation: Golden Cabinet Kidney Qi Pill · Eastern Hàn dynasty, circa 200 CE
formulas.properties: Warm, Tonifies Kidney Yang, Warms Yang and Transforms Qi, Warms the Ming Men Fire
formulas.description: A classical formula that gently warms and supports the Kidneys to restore vitality, fluid balance, and lower body warmth. It is used for people with Kidney weakness who experience lower back soreness, cold legs, frequent urination or difficulty urinating, and general fatigue. Unlike strong warming formulas, it uses a small amount of warming herbs alongside a larger base of nourishing ingredients, working gradually to restore the body's natural balance.

faqs.question: How does TCM treat wheezing differently from a rescue inhaler?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to resolve the root cause, not just open the airways temporarily. Herbs and acupuncture address the specific imbalance - whether it's cold phlegm, heat phlegm, or weak lungs - so that over time the wheezing becomes less frequent and less severe. An inhaler provides immediate relief during an attack, but TCM works to prevent those attacks from happening in the first place.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with exercise-induced wheezing?
faqs.answer: Yes, especially when the underlying pattern is Lung Qi Deficiency or Kidney Qi Deficiency. By strengthening the body's Qi, TCM can improve exercise tolerance and reduce post-exertion wheezing. Your practitioner will select herbs and points to tonify the Lungs and Kidneys, helping you breathe more deeply and recover more quickly.

faqs.question: Is it safe to use herbs alongside my asthma medication?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, but it's crucial to inform both your TCM practitioner and your doctor. Some herbs, like Ma Huang (ephedra), can interact with bronchodilators or heart medications, so professional supervision is essential. Never stop your prescribed inhalers or steroids abruptly. With coordinated care, many patients successfully integrate both approaches.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I have wheezing?
faqs.answer: In general, avoid cold, raw, and greasy foods that promote phlegm production. Dairy, cold drinks, and heavy sweets can worsen phlegm. Favor warm, cooked foods and drinks like ginger tea. Specific recommendations depend on your pattern - for example, pears are helpful for Phlegm-Heat but may aggravate Cold-Phlegm - so personalized dietary advice is best.

faqs.question: How long does it take for herbs to stop the wheezing?
faqs.answer: For acute attacks, herbs can bring relief within days. For chronic wheezing, it may take several weeks to clear phlegm and months to strengthen underlying deficiencies. Consistency is key, and your formula will be adjusted as your condition evolves.

faqs.question: Will the wheezing come back after TCM treatment?
faqs.answer: TCM aims to correct the underlying imbalance, so recurrence is less likely than with symptomatic treatment alone. However, if you return to habits that created the imbalance - such as a poor diet, overwork, or chronic stress - symptoms may reappear. Maintenance care and lifestyle adjustments can help prevent relapses.

research.title: Acupuncture for chronic asthma
research.description: A Cochrane systematic review including 12 randomized controlled trials with 350 participants. The review found no significant difference between real and sham acupuncture for asthma symptoms, lung function, or medication use. However, some individual trials suggested acupuncture may improve quality of life and reduce bronchodilator use.
research.periodical: McCarney RW, Brinkhaus B, Lasserson TJ, Linde K. Acupuncture for chronic asthma. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2004, Issue 1. Art. No.: CD000008.

research.title: Efficacy and safety of modified Ding-Chuan-Tang in asthmatic children with airway hyper-responsiveness: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial
research.description: This trial evaluated modified Ding Chuan Tang in 60 asthmatic children with airway hyper-responsiveness. After 12 weeks, the herbal group showed significant improvement in pulmonary function and symptom scores compared to placebo, with no serious adverse events. The study supports the traditional use of Ding Chuan Tang for Phlegm-Heat wheezing in children.
research.periodical: Hsu CH, Lu CM, Chang TT. Efficacy and safety of modified Ding-Chuan-Tang in asthmatic children with airway hyper-responsiveness: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial. Pediatric Pulmonology 2006; 41(5): 472-479.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for asthma: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials
research.description: This systematic review analyzed 22 RCTs involving 2,430 participants. It concluded that Chinese herbal medicine, as an adjunct to conventional therapy, significantly improved lung function and reduced asthma symptoms compared to placebo or conventional treatment alone. The review noted the need for better methodological quality in future studies.
research.periodical: Shergis JL, Wu L, Zhang AL, Guo X, Lu C, Xue CC. Chinese herbal medicine for asthma: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials. Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine 2011; 17(8): 683-691.
